name: Hassan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build stairs and do the finer joinery for a small builder, Hartmann Homes, that makes custom houses, maybe eight or ten a year, for people who want something properly made. Oak stairs, handrails, built-in bookshelves, sometimes a big front door. Now and then we do repairs on old buildings, and last spring I rebuilt the gallery stairs in St Joseph's, our parish church, which I'm prouder of than anything. I start at seven, I have a workshop in the yard behind the site office, and I listen to the radio while I cut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about the job do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a client walks up a stair I built and says nothing, just runs a hand along the rail. That's the best review there is. What wears me out is the young site managers who want everything yesterday and send me messages on a phone I barely use. I don't touch computers, my wife Marta does our bills, and I've been married to her thirty-four years, so that system works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, a machine can't love the wood. Somebody always comes along promising the end of hard work, and here we are. At church on Sunday I'd say it to the men after Mass and we'd laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish my working life the way I started it. I've got the house, our savings, and a few years left at Hartmann's. My son Daniel is a plasterer, and he'd be fine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, nothing different. Keep building stairs, keep saving, and maybe take on one more apprentice before I go, if Mr Hartmann agrees. I'd retire at sixty-three or sixty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Satisfied, even, like I was right to be stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why another apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to know how to cut a stair string by hand when I'm gone. I learned from my uncle, and he learned from his. You pay it back by teaching, that's how a trade stays alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI saves a bit of time somewhere, where would that be at Hartmann's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the office, with the drawings and quotes, I suppose. Mr Hartmann's daughter does all that now on her laptop. As long as she doesn't ask me to look at it, I don't mind.

S0.say: I'd say a machine can't love the wood and someone always promises the end of hard work. I'd laugh about it with the men after Mass.
S0.think: It means I finish my working life the way I started. I've got the house, savings and a few years left, and my son would be fine too.
S0.do: Carries on building stairs and saving at Hartmann Homes. Hopes to take on one more apprentice before retiring at sixty-three or sixty-four.
S0.feel: Calm and satisfied, as if his stubbornness was proven right.
S0.quote: Because somebody has to know how to cut a stair string by hand when I'm gone.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan's identity is the craft and its passing down through apprentices. He's comfortable with others using computers so long as he doesn't have to. His parish and family come up constantly as his real community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a handmade stair, and a machine's stair is a factory stair. Some will go for cheap, sure, they always have. I'd tell the young ones to learn a real skill with their hands, not chase screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm a bit worried for Daniel. Plastering is the kind of thing they might get a machine to spray. And I'm worried the apprentices stop coming, because why spend four years learning if a machine might do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my work exactly as I do, I'm not changing at fifty-eight. I'd talk to Daniel about moving towards restoration work, old houses, lime plaster, the things a machine can't figure out. And I'd keep teaching my apprentice, Luka, the hand skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for my son. For me, not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, learn lime plaster and old work, because rich people and churches will always pay for that. Don't be the man who does what a machine does, only slower. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd listen eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible, if apprentices stopped coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the schools, they've told kids for thirty years that a trade is for failures. And partly the parents who believed them. You can't blame a machine for that.

S1.say: I'd say people still want handmade stairs and a machine's stair is a factory stair. I'd tell young people to learn real hand skills, not chase screens.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried for Daniel, since a machine might spray plaster. And I worry apprentices stop coming if a machine might do the job.
S1.do: Keeps working exactly as he does and refuses to change tools at fifty-eight. Urges his son towards restoration and lime plaster work and keeps teaching his apprentice hand skills.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy for his son, not much for himself.
S1.quote: Don't be the man who does what a machine does, only slower.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan's answer to change is to retreat further into craft and steer his son there too. He blames schools and parents for devaluing trades, not companies or technology. He's firm that he won't change himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say God made us to work, and a world where nobody works is a sick world. I'd say it at church, at the builders' merchant, to anyone. And I'd say the government shouldn't just hand everybody money, it should make sure people have something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would break something in me, to be honest. Not the money, Marta and I have enough. But my son, my apprentice, the men from the parish who work on sites, all of them with nothing to get up for. I'd lie awake thinking about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as anyone would pay for a handmade stair, even if it was half the work. I'd put money aside to help Daniel and his wife with their mortgage if he lost his work, before I'd let him take a handout. And I'd talk to Father Michael about the parish doing something, a workshop or a jobs group for the men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's going out from under the whole street, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep working even at half the work. Would you learn to use the new tools to stay in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've thought about it, and no. If I'm going to finish, I'll finish with my own hands, not supervising a machine. That's pride, maybe, but it's all I've got that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help Daniel before letting him take a handout. If there was a public income for everyone, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. My head says no, it's not earned. But if everyone gets it and the work's gone, then I suppose I'd be a fool to refuse, and I'd put it in the collection plate.

S2.say: I'd say God made us to work and a world where nobody works is sick. Government shouldn't just hand out money, it should make sure people have something to do.
S2.think: It would break something in me, not for money but for my son, my apprentice and the men in the parish with nothing to get up for. I'd lie awake over that.
S2.do: Keeps working as long as anyone pays for a handmade stair and sets money aside to help his son's mortgage rather than see him take a handout. Asks the parish priest about a workshop or jobs group for the men.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground is going out from under the whole street.
S2.quote: If I'm going to finish, I'll finish with my own hands, not supervising a machine.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan's alarm is about meaning and community, not income, since his savings are solid. He refuses to adapt even to stay working, and was honest it's pride. His answer on a public income was torn, and his solution was the collection plate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, a world without work is a sick world. But with five years, families and churches can get ready, and young people can choose trades that last. I'd say it plainly, no politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years almost gets me to the end. I'd finish at Hartmann's and step away. It's Daniel and Luka I'd lose sleep over, more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside each month, so we can help Daniel if it comes to that. I'd help Luka finish his apprenticeship early, push him to qualify in two years instead of four. I'd keep working the same way to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for the young ones. Not panicking, but carrying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why rush Luka's apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So he has his papers before it all changes. A qualified joiner can do repair work, restoration, things people pay for by the hour. An apprentice who's half done has nothing to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no politics. Would you vote differently, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I vote the way I always have, for the people who believe in work and family. I'd want them to back apprenticeships, not handouts. But I'm not going to stand on a box about it.

S3.say: I'd say a world without work is sick, but five years lets families and churches get ready and lets young people choose trades that last.
S3.think: Five years almost gets me to the end, so I'd finish and step away. It's Daniel and Luka I'd lose sleep over.
S3.do: Saves a bit more each month to help his son if needed and pushes his apprentice to qualify in two years instead of four. Keeps working the same way to the end.
S3.feel: Anxious for the young ones, carrying it but not panicking.
S3.quote: An apprentice who's half done has nothing to show.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Hassan's plan becomes concrete: get his apprentice qualified fast and keep money ready for his son. His values, work and family over public support, stay constant. He wants his party to back apprenticeships but won't campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and plenty of these predictions come to nothing. If it comes, families and parishes will look after each other, like they always have. I'd say that at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's past my working years, I'd be sixty-eight. I'll be in the garden or fixing the church benches. I worry about it in a quiet way, like you worry about your grandchildren's world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Finish at Hartmann's, teach Luka everything, retire. Maybe I'd keep a small workshop at home and make furniture for the parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Not for me, for the people after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you have grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two, Daniel's girls, six and three. I'd like them to learn to make something with their hands, even if they never need to. I'd teach them to make a stool, like my uncle taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking at all five, has anything in your thinking shifted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I believe what I believed when we sat down. Work is good for a man, and a machine can't love the wood.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long and many predictions come to nothing. If it comes, families and parishes will look after each other as they always have.
S4.think: It's past my working years, so I'll be in the garden or fixing church benches. I worry quietly, like you worry about your grandchildren's world.
S4.do: Finishes at Hartmann Homes after teaching his apprentice everything, then retires. Plans a small home workshop making furniture for the parish.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy, not for himself but for those who come after.
S4.quote: I'd teach them to make a stool, like my uncle taught me.
S4.fieldNote: Hassan's position barely moved across the five scenarios, and he said so himself. Even safely retired in this version, he carries a low worry for his granddaughters. Passing skills down is his constant theme.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A whole street of men with nothing to do, that's what frightens me, more than any money. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going and paying people to do real work, repairing old buildings, churches, schools, instead of just sending them a cheque. And families sticking together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people will need something to hold on to if this happens. It'll be the churches and the families picking people up, not the computer companies.

headlineQuote: It'll be the churches and the families picking people up, not the computer companies.
portrait: Hassan Lopez is a 58-year-old stair builder and joiner for a small custom home builder, a man of faith who rebuilt the gallery stairs in his parish church and has never touched a computer. Financially secure, with a house and savings, his worries are about meaning, his plasterer son, his apprentice and the men in his parish. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy in steady change, but the two-year AGI scenario alarms him because it would leave a whole street without work to get up for. He refuses to adapt even to stay working, steers his son towards restoration, and trusts family and church over handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because a whole street of men with nothing to do frightens him more than any money.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships going and paying people for real work like repairing old buildings, churches and schools, rather than just sending a cheque, plus families sticking together.
